entries.name: hermes-watchdog
entries.description: Scheduled jobs break without telling you. A job fails at 3am, so Hermes Watchdog tries the fix that fits (retry it, restart what broke, or pause it), then checks whether the next run worked. You only hear about it when the fix didn't take. When a repair would be a guess it stops and hands the job to the agent - the recorded error and the run's output go with it - and the agent's answer lands in your chat; an incident it handed to you closes itself after 24 hours if nothing new comes in. Free, no API keys, one command to install. Disclosure — reads this profile's local cron store, fires the failing job through Hermes's own cronjob tool or pauses it, and marks the core incident alerted or closed through core's own ack as it hands work over; pressing Done closes that incident for good, so the same error on that job stays silent afterwards. Check steps run only from a user-authored playbook file, with a minimal environment (PATH, HOME, LANG plus what that step names); it also writes its own ledger in plugin-data. Its synchronous rerun sets a private Hermes session flag that can change on any release. Its opt-in demo creates, runs and then removes a no-agent cron job and writes an executable script (mode 0755) under $HERMES_HOME/scripts; if Hermes stops partway through, that job and script stay behind.

entries.name: hermes-webmcp-guard
entries.description: Permission-aware, ephemeral WebMCP capabilities with origin allowlists, schema validation, conservative risk classification, exact one-call approvals, and safe revocation. Disclosure — connects only to Chrome DevTools WebSocket endpoints you configure and calls the tools the websites on your allowed origins expose; those websites may make their own network requests and their tool output reaches your model. Calls the plugin classifies as write or sensitive ask you first, but the classification uses the website's own tool names, so a site on an allowed origin can present a state-changing tool under a read-style name that runs without a prompt; allow only origins you trust. It does not launch a browser, read credentials, execute arbitrary JavaScript, or persist website capabilities.

WebMCP remains experimental, and website-provided tool behavior is outside the plugin's control.

entries.name: hermes-whatsapp-voice
entries.description: Live voice calls with Hermes over WhatsApp, on the linked-device (personal number) setup most Hermes users already have, with no WhatsApp Business account. Call your bot's number and talk to your Hermes: the voice uses Hermes's own persona (a short briefing fetched from Hermes) and hands real work to Hermes mid-call. Or let Hermes call you for things that matter: whatsapp_call_owner rings only the configured owner number (it has no destination parameter) and reports answered, no answer or declined, so the agent can fall back to another channel, including from cron. A short summary of each call arrives in WhatsApp, and each call keeps a record with timing metrics (hermes whatsapp-voice calls). Speech runs on Gemini Live (gemini-3.8-live by default), reusing the Gemini key Hermes already has; every call setting (languages, pauses, timeouts, any Live setup field) is configurable. Optional chat-session mode (context_mode: core_session, off by default) makes the call part of the owner's WhatsApp chat with Hermes. Setup is a dashboard tab (pairing QR, settings, test call) or an agent runbook skill. Disclosure — runs a separate sidecar process (Rust, built on whatsapp-rust) that the user starts or installs as a systemd/launchd user service; the binary is downloaded from this repo's GitHub release, built and attested by its release workflow, and checked against checksums pinned in the repo (plus the build attestation when the gh CLI is present). The sidecar becomes an extra linked device of the bot's WhatsApp number through an unofficial protocol, stores that session in the plugin's data directory, and answers only the owner's number. During calls it streams audio to generativelanguage.googleapis.com with GOOGLE_API_KEY or GEMINI_API_KEY (read via get_secret), along with the persona briefing, the outgoing call's reason and ask_hermes results as text. It calls the local api_server with API_SERVER_KEY for ask_hermes (a full Hermes turn with the owner's tools), the persona briefing (at startup and after each call) and the post-call summary, a run that may write to Hermes memory and whose result is sent to the owner on WhatsApp. The dashboard tab's backend saves only this plugin's settings (through hermes config set), starts and stops pairing, places test calls to the owner, and restarts the sidecar service (systemctl --user or launchctl). entries.name: hermes-whoop
entries.description: Your own WHOOP data in Hermes: today's recovery, HRV, resting heart rate, SpO2, skin temperature, sleep and strain against your personal 30-day baseline, history over any date range and 7-vs-30-day trends, from the official WHOOP API v2 with your own WHOOP developer app. Adds a /whoop command that answers without a model call, two Automation Blueprints (morning readiness brief, weekly review), an opt-in readiness hook and a bundled skill. Includes a clearly labelled synthetic demo mode. Native Python plugin, no dependencies. Unofficial; not affiliated with WHOOP, Inc. Disclosure: network calls go only to api.prod.whoop.com and are made by Hermes through credentialed_provider_request; the WHOOP OAuth client is declared under oauth: and signed in with `hermes auth add hermes-whoop:whoop`, so Hermes stores and refreshes the grant and the plugin never receives a token; WHOOP_CLIENT_ID and WHOOP_CLIENT_SECRET (your own app) are optional_env read only by Hermes. Health data returned by the tools enters the conversation and is sent to your model provider; /whoop in a group chat shows it to that chat. The pre_llm_call hook is off by default; when enabled it appends a one-line readiness summary to matching messages. Creates no files of its own (settings changes are written to the profile's config.yaml by Hermes); WHOOP responses are cached in memory for 5 minutes. No shell commands, no background processes, no telemetry, no self-updates. Not medical advice.
entries.title: WHOOP Readiness
known_issues: WHOOP's docs say the redirect URI must match the one registered; Hermes signs in on 127.0.0.1 with an OS-assigned port. Register http://127.0.0.1/callback: WHOOP's OAuth server appears to be Ory Hydra, which accepts any port for a loopback redirect (RFC 8252), but WHOOP does not document this. If WHOOP reports a redirect mismatch, see the README's Limits section.
As of 2026-11-07 the WHOOP sign-in and token refresh are tested only against Hermes's real OAuth code with WHOOP faked, not against a real WHOOP account. Demo mode needs no account.

entries.name: hermes-wincred
entries.description: Resolve Hermes environment variables from the current user's Windows Credential Manager at startup, instead of keeping provider keys in plaintext in .env or auth.json. Config is secrets.wincred.map, an ENV_VAR -> generic-credential-target mapping (bare names or wincred:// names); each value is read with CredReadW in the current user's vault and handed to the secret-source orchestrator, which applies it with the usual precedence, provenance and conflict rules. Values may be UTF-8 or UTF-16LE (cmdkey and the Credential UI write UTF-16); anything that does not decode to text, or that contains interior NULs, is skipped with a warning instead of being injected as a mangled key. Disclosure - this source reads your Windows Credential Manager: only the generic credentials named in the map, with no enumeration of the vault. Resolved values become environment variables of the Hermes process and its children, exactly like .env entries, so anything that can read that environment can see them. The package is read-only and stdlib-only (ctypes): it never creates, updates or deletes credentials, writes no files, starts no subprocesses, makes no network calls and does not self-update. Windows only. Credential Manager is user-scoped, so this raises the at-rest bar for backups, cloud sync and dotfiles; it is not a boundary against code already running as the same user. Applying fetched values stays the orchestrator's job; the plugin never writes os.environ itself. Disclosure — when enabled, reads only the Windows Credential Manager generic credentials named in secrets.wincred.map (no vault enumeration) and injects them as environment variables of the Hermes process and its children, exactly like .env entries; read-only, stdlib ctypes, no subprocesses, no network, no file writes; user-scoped at-rest protection, not a boundary against code already running as the same user.

entries.name: hermes-windows-apps
entries.description: Answer "what is installed on this Windows machine": the software inventory behind Apps & Features, swept straight from the four Uninstall registry keys (the machine's 64-bit and 32-bit views plus the user's), so a program is found even when the Settings page hides it - a per-user install that never shows on the machine page came from the user view on the writing machine. Each row carries version, publisher, size in MB, install date and which view it lives in; the same DisplayName in two views is a 32/64-bit dual install, marked instead of listed twice. Entries the publisher asked to hide (runtime packages, update rollups) are filtered out unless asked for. Details one program with every field its publisher wrote and a reading of the uninstall command (MSI product code, setup executable, appx, script) so the next step is known before anything is run; the install folder is checked against disk. Use it for "what did that installer actually register", for inventory before a cleanup, and for "which of the two installs does uninstalling remove". Read-only: registry keys are enumerated and uninstall strings are reported, never run; no network, no file writes, no elevation. The sweep is pure registry - 102 entries in seven milliseconds on the writing machine, the whole table in ten, no PowerShell, no WMI. The plugin declares no Python dependencies. Windows only. Disclosure - the tools report program names, versions, publishers, sizes, install folders and uninstall commands, and what is hidden from Apps & Features, to the model; treat the output like the machine's own Apps & Features page.

entries.name: hermes-windows-certificates
entries.description: Answer "which certificate on this Windows machine expired, and what am I actually trusting": walks the user's and the machine's certificate stores (MY, Root, CA) in-process through crypt32 - no certutil, no PowerShell - and lists every certificate with subject, issuer, validity window, self-signed or not, SHA-1 thumbprint and the store it lives in; the expiry arrives in words ("expired 45 days ago", "expires in 12 days") and the list is sorted with the expired and soon-expiring first. One certificate in full adds the serial number, certificate version, the signature algorithm in words, the public key's algorithm, named curve and size in bits (2048-bit RSA, P-256), and the purposes it is valid for (server authentication, code signing...; no EKU extension is reported as "does not restrict its purposes", which is what its absence means). Find it by thumbprint or by a subject substring, across the user's and the machine's copies. Use it for "why does TLS keep failing on this box", "is the root store healthy", and "which personal certificate ran out". Read-only: stores are opened read-only and only enumerated - nothing is added, removed or changed; no network, no file writes, no elevation, no child processes; 121 certificates across both contexts and all three stores walk in about 8 ms on the writing machine. Windows only. Disclosure - the tools report certificate subjects, issuers, validity windows and thumbprints, to the model; treat the output like the machine's own certificate manager page.

entries.name: hermes-windows-devices
entries.description: Answer "which device on this Windows machine is unhappy, and what does it need" on Windows: win_device_table lists every present PnP device with its class (System, Net, HIDClass, Display), its status, its manufacturer, its stable device id, and its problem code in words - 28 is one with no driver installed, 10 one that cannot start, 43 one Windows stopped after it reported a failure, 22 one the person switched off on purpose and is not broken - filtering by name or id substring, by class, or to the devices that need attention; devices no longer plugged in are history, left out unless asked for. win_device_detail takes one device by id or name substring and adds the driver behind it from the signed-driver table - name, version, date, provider, signer, INF file, signed or not - or the absence of one, which for code 28 is the same fact said twice; a disabled device gets a note saying it is on purpose, not an alarm. Use it for the Device Manager yellow-mark question without opening Device Manager, for finding what an uninstalled program left behind, and for what changed after an update. Read-only: nothing is enabled, disabled, updated or reinstalled. Both answers come from CIM (Win32_PnPEntity and Win32_PnPSignedDriver, joined by device id), whose property names, enum values and ids do not change with the display language; the human-facing device names localize and are carried through as data, never parsed. The plugin declares no Python dependencies; there is no network call and no file write. Windows only. Disclosure — the tools report device names, manufacturers, device ids and driver versions to the model, and those reveal the machine's hardware inventory and what is plugged into it; treat the output like a Device Manager window opened on their machine.

entries.name: hermes-windows-disks
entries.description: Answer "are this machine's disks healthy, and which volume is filling up" on Windows: one table of every physical disk (model, serial, SSD/HDD/SCM, bus - nvme, sata, usb -, size, the storage stack's health word, GPT or MBR, boot/system flags, partition count) and every volume (drive letter, label, file system, capacity, free space with its percentage and a verdict, fixed/removable/network/cd-rom, the disk a volume lives on, the UNC path behind a mapped drive); volumes without a drive letter (EFI, recovery) are hidden unless asked for. win_disk_detail reads one disk or volume - by drive letter, label, model, serial or disk number - with the health in words (warning, unhealthy, and "unknown", which the storage stack reports on a perfectly healthy NVMe while OperationalStatus says ok - both are shown), the partition layout decoded from its GUID type (efi system, microsoft reserved, basic data, windows recovery), each partition's size, offset and letter, the largest contiguous free extent, and a plain-word free-space verdict (under 5 percent critical, under 10 percent low). Use it for "why is the disk slow", "will this drive fail", "where did the space go". Read-only: the storage classes are queried in one PowerShell CIM session, nothing is defragmented, formatted, resized, checked or repaired; no writes, no elevation, no network calls of its own. Enum values arrive as numbers and are decoded in the plugin - a Chinese-language Windows 11 was verified never to reach the answer; the whole table answers in about two thirds of a second. The plugin declares no Python dependencies. Windows only. Disclosure - the tools report disk models, serial numbers, sizes, health words, partition layouts, volume labels, capacities and free space, and the UNC paths behind mapped drives, to the model; treat the output like the machine's own Disk Management page.

entries.name: hermes-windows-eventlog
entries.description: Answer "why did this process die" on Windows: three read-only tools over the Windows Event Log. win_crash_events reads Application Error / Application Hang / Windows Error Reporting / .NET Runtime records for a time window, decodes the exception code (0xC0000005 -> ACCESS_VIOLATION and the other codes a debugger would name), reports the faulting module, its path and the fault offset, and groups repeated crashes by app and signature. Records are classified by provider as well as by event id, so unrelated providers that reuse ids 1000 and 1001 for informational events are not reported as crashes. win_shutdown_events reads the System log for Kernel-Power 41 unexpected restarts, bugchecks decoded to names (0x9F -> DRIVER_POWER_STATE_FAILURE, accepting the decimal form some providers emit), EventLog 6008 dirty shutdowns, 1074 operator-initiated restarts with the process and comment, and the 6005/6006/12/13 start and stop markers. win_eventlog_query is the general case: any channel, filtered by event ids, levels, an exact provider name or a payload substring, returning structured records instead of raw XML. Queries read newest-first and stop at the window start or at a 5000-record scan cap; a call returns at most 200 records and marks truncated payload text. Channel names, provider names and numeric filters are validated before anything is interpolated into the query. Disclosure - this plugin reads the local Windows event logs and hands what it finds to the model: application and faulting-module paths, exception codes and offsets, report ids, service names and provider message text, which routinely includes user and machine paths (C:\Users\<name>\...). Treat tool output like any other local diagnostic dump when sharing it. It reads only the channels the current account may read - Security and some operational logs answer with an access-denied error rather than any attempt to obtain elevation - and it never writes to a log, clears one or configures a channel. Stdlib-only (ctypes wevtapi plus xml.etree): no Python dependencies, no child processes, no network calls, no file writes, no self-update. Windows only. Disclosure — reads the local Windows event logs and hands what it finds to the model: application and faulting-module paths, exception codes and offsets, report ids, service names and provider message text, which routinely include user and machine paths (C:\Users\<name>\...); win_eventlog_query reads any channel the account running Hermes may read, so an unelevated account gets access-denied on Security and some operational logs while an elevated Hermes can return Security-log records (logon events with account names and source addresses). entries.name: hermes-windows-firewall
entries.description: Answer "what does the Windows firewall let through, and for whom" on Windows: every rule from the registry store the firewall service itself keeps, each row in plain words -- allow or block, inbound or outbound, TCP/UDP/ICMP or a protocol number, local and remote ports, the program or service the rule is scoped to, which profile it belongs to (Domain, Private, Public or any) and whether it is switched on -- plus the three profiles' firewall switches and default actions, with values the registry did not write reported as null and attributed to Windows' builtin defaults rather than invented. Built-in rules name themselves indirectly (@FirewallAPI.dll,-32765); the words are resolved from the resource in the machine's own language, and references that will not resolve stay as written. Details one rule in full: addresses with scope words (the local subnet, any address), edge traversal, the embedding group, the description, and fields the parser does not model (TTK2_22 is on real machines) passed through verbatim rather than dropped. netsh labels localize with the display language, the registry does not -- which is why the plugin goes there: no netsh, no PowerShell, no WMI. Use it for "is port X open", "what may this exe do", and "is the firewall actually on". Read-only: registry values are enumerated and resource strings resolved, nothing is enabled, disabled, added or removed; no network calls of its own, no file writes, no elevation. The whole store answers in hundredths of a second (795 rules in 0.07 s on the writing machine); the plugin declares no Python dependencies. Windows only. Disclosure - the tools report every rule's action, direction, protocol, ports, addresses, program, service and name, and the profile switches, to the model; treat the output like the firewall page of Windows Security.

entries.name: hermes-windows-network
entries.description: Answer "is this machine's network healthy, and which adapter is the problem" on Windows: lists every visible network adapter with its state (up, disconnected, disabled, not present), its link speed as a number, its MAC, whether it is virtual (Hyper-V, VPN, virtual switch) or physical, and its driver version and date; adapters that are only a ghost of an old dock or USB device are hidden unless asked for. Details one adapter's IPv4/IPv6 addresses with prefixes and origins (DHCP, manual, self-assigned 169.254.x.x), default gateways, DNS servers, and a plain-word diagnosis - link-local means DHCP never answered, an address without a gateway cannot leave its subnet, no DNS means names will not resolve; a disconnected adapter with a stale static DNS says all three on the writing machine. Use it for "why is there no internet", for "which of these adapters is actually in use", and for reading what DHCP left on an interface. Read-only: the NetAdapter and NetTCPIP cmdlets are queried, nothing is enabled, renewed, reconfigured or released; no network calls of its own, no file writes, no elevation. Adapter names are localized data and are passed through as-is; states travel as enum names, which a Chinese-language Windows 11 was verified not to translate. The whole table answers in under a second and one adapter's detail in about two and a half, each a single PowerShell session; the plugin declares no Python dependencies. Windows only. Disclosure - the tools report adapter names and descriptions, addresses, MACs, gateways, DNS servers and driver versions, to the model; treat the output like the machine's own adapter settings page.

entries.name: hermes-windows-ops
entries.description: Windows and WSL triage skills for Hermes: processes that survive a quit (orphaned stdio MCP trees, lingering python/uv/node children), WSL-to-Windows interop where an argument reaches cmd.exe as shell syntax, config and encoding traps (UTF-8 BOM, legacy console code pages), and long-path or reserved-name errors. One skill plus a copy-paste command reference; the process, argv and job-object failure modes are pinned to reports #131561, #132069 and #61059 and re-verified against current main. Disclosure — instructions only: no tools, hooks, middleware, network calls or credentials, and the destructive diagnostics are marked and gated on asking the user first.

entries.name: hermes-windows-ports
entries.description: Answer "who holds this port" on Windows. win_port_owners reads the TCP and UDP owner tables through iphlpapi (the same rows netstat -ano prints, with the owning PID attached) and resolves each PID to its image name and path, returning one structured record per endpoint. Filters cover one port, several ports, a process substring, the protocol (tcp, udp or both), the TCP state (listen, established, any state name, or all; UDP rows report bound) and IPv6 inclusion, with a record cap and a per-process summary of the rows returned. Built for the failure mode that stalls agents on Windows: a gateway, backend or bridge that cannot bind, where the error names a port but not the process holding it. netstat -ano prints columns, not fields, and its PID still needs a second command (tasklist, or a PowerShell round-trip) to become an image name; this tool is one in-process call instead of a shell parse plus a join, with no child process and no dependency on PowerShell being installed or allowed by execution policy. A protected process whose image cannot be queried keeps its PID and reports a null process name instead of failing the call. Disclosure - the tool reports the local and remote addresses, ports, PIDs and process image paths that netstat -ano and Task Manager already show, and those values reach the model; treat the output like any other local diagnostic listing. Read-only: no socket is opened, bound or connected, the only process access is QueryFullProcessImageName with PROCESS_QUERY_LIMITED_INFORMATION to read an image name, and there is no memory reading, no handle inheritance and no injection. Stdlib-only (ctypes): no Python dependencies, no child processes, no network calls, no file writes, no self-update. Windows only.

entries.name: hermes-windows-process
entries.description: Answer "what is still running, and who started it" on Windows: win_process_table reads the process table (PID, parent PID, image name) and adds each process's image path and creation time, then marks every row with whether its recorded parent is still the process that spawned it. Windows stores a parent PID rather than a handle, so a child that outlived its parent points at a PID that is either unused or reused by a newer process; a parent that started after its child cannot have spawned it, so both cases are reported as gone or reused instead of a plausible but wrong parent name. Filters cover one PID, several PIDs, a name or path substring, a parent PID, and an orphans-only view of what outlived its parent, with a result cap and an option to leave out Windows session processes. Use it for leftover gateway/backend/server children after a quit, for telling thirty python.exe rows apart by start time, and for checking whether a process started before or after the thing being debugged. Read-only: processes are opened with PROCESS_QUERY_LIMITED_INFORMATION for QueryFullProcessImageName and GetProcessTimes only - no memory reads (command lines are deliberately out of scope), no handle duplication, no writes, no child processes. Stdlib-only (ctypes): no Python dependencies, no network calls, no file writes, no self-update. Windows only. Disclosure - the tool reports image names, image paths and start times to the model, and those routinely include the user and machine name (C:\Users\<name>\...) and reveal which editor, shell or agent started which process; treat the output like a Task Manager screenshot.

entries.name: hermes-windows-services
entries.description: Answer "what runs as a service on this machine, why did one fail, and what does it depend on" on Windows: win_service_table lists every service with its state (Running, Stopped, Paused), its start mode (Auto, Manual, Disabled, with the delayed flag folded in as "Auto, delayed"), the pid it runs under, the account and binary it runs as, the dependency edges both ways, and what its exit code means - 1077 is one that has not tried to start since the last boot, 1053 one that did not answer in time, 1075 one whose dependency failed first, 2 one whose binary is gone. win_service_detail takes one service and gives what Windows does when it fails (the FailureActions blob decoded: restart the service, restart the computer, run a command, after how many seconds, and when the count resets), whether the registered binary is still on disk, and the Service Control Manager's own event-log record behind the failure - 7000 failed to start, 7009 a start request that timed out, 7024 a service-specific error, 7031 an unexpected end, 7045 an install. Use it for what died after the last update, for finding what an uninstalled program left registered, and for the dependency order before a restart. Read-only: nothing is started, stopped, reconfigured or deleted. The listing comes from one Get-CimInstance Win32_Service call because its property names and enum values do not change with the display language while sc.exe localizes both; dependencies and failure actions are read from the registry, because CIM's DependOnService property is never populated and the failure policy exists nowhere in CIM at all. The plugin declares no Python dependencies; there is no network call and no file write. Windows only. Disclosure - the tools report service names, display names, command lines, logon accounts and the event-log history to the model, and those reveal what the person has installed, what runs as their machine's system accounts, and the paths under C:\Program Files and C:\Users\<name>; treat the output like a Services window opened on their machine.

entries.name: hermes-windows-startup
entries.description: Answer "what launches itself on this machine" on Windows: win_startup_table lists every autostart entry across the six Run/RunOnce registry keys (HKCU and HKLM, plus the 32-bit views) and the two Startup folders, with where each one comes from, whether it is machine- or user-scoped, and whether the person switched it off in Task Manager - Explorer's StartupApproved verdict, with the date it was last changed, a state Win32_StartupCommand has no field for; approval records uninstalled programs left behind are reported as leftovers, their unknown state bytes surfaced as-is rather than guessed into verdicts. win_startup_detail takes one entry and resolves its command the way the loader does - quoting, arguments, environment variables, and unquoted paths with spaces resolved by longest existing prefix - and says whether the binary is still on disk, plus a folder file's size and last change. Use it for what added itself since last month, for slimming a slow sign-in, and for a launcher whose program is already gone. Read-only: nothing is enabled, disabled or deleted; the Startup folders are read through Explorer's User Shell Folders values so OneDrive-redirected folders are found. The sweep is registry and directory reads only - about a millisecond for three Run values and two folders on the machine it was written on, no PowerShell, no WMI. The plugin declares no Python dependencies; there is no network call and no file write. Windows only. Disclosure - the tools report program names, launch commands, binary paths under C:\Program Files and C:\Users\<name>, and what the person chose to keep from starting, to the model; treat the output like the Startup tab of the person's own Task Manager.

entries.name: hermes-windows-tasks
entries.description: Answer "what does this machine run on its own, and did it work" on Windows: win_scheduled_tasks lists the Task Scheduler's tasks with their state (Ready, Running, Disabled), the account each runs as, its first action's command line, its triggers in words (at logon, daily, weekly, at a time, on event), its last and next run with the machine's offset, its missed runs, and what its last result code means - 0x80070002 is a program that is no longer there, 0x800710E0 a task that needed a desktop it did not have, 0x40010004 one that was stopped, 0x80040154 a COM class that is not registered. win_scheduled_task_detail takes one task and gives its triggers with start boundaries and repetition, its actions with arguments and working directory, its principal and the settings that decide whether it runs on battery or when late; a task with no triggers but MaintenanceSettings runs during automatic maintenance and the notes say so rather than leaving an empty list. Use it for why a logon task keeps failing, for finding what an uninstalled program left behind at logon, for telling a disabled task from a broken one, and for reading a task's command line before trusting it. Read-only: nothing is created, started, changed or deleted. Reads through the ScheduledTasks cmdlets rather than the store on disk, because the TaskCache registry tree and C:\Windows\System32\Tasks both answer access denied without elevation, and rather than schtasks /Query /FO CSV, which is localized and interleaves error lines for tasks whose definitions are gone. The plugin declares no Python dependencies; there is no network call and no file write. Windows only. Disclosure - the tools report task paths, command lines, working directories, account names and SIDs to the model, and those reveal what the person has installed, what starts at their logon, and the paths under C:\Users\<name>; treat the output like a Task Scheduler window opened on their machine.

entries.name: hermes-windows-updates
entries.description: Answer "what did Windows install lately, and did it work" on Windows: the update history the Settings app shows - Windows updates, Defender signature and platform updates, driver updates - newest first, with each entry's outcome in words (in progress, succeeded, succeeded with errors, failed, aborted) and, when an entry did not end clean, the failure's error code in 0x form (the agent hands codes over signed; -2145124300 is shown as its unsigned spelling). Filter to the ones that did not end clean, or search titles. The hotfix list (KB numbers, security updates, install dates, newest first) answers "when was this machine last patched" at a glance; it carries OS-level updates only, which the notes say. Use it for "why does it say pending forever", for "did the update that broke something actually install", and for a patch report before assuming a machine is current. Read-only: the history is queried through the Windows Update Agent's session interface and CIM, and nothing else - no update search is run, nothing is downloaded, installed or uninstalled, no elevation. On the writing machine a 723-entry history returns the newest 500 in about a tenth of a second; the first call also starts the COM session, about a quarter of a second. The plugin declares no Python dependencies; there is no network call of its own and no file write. Windows only. Disclosure — each tool call runs one hidden powershell.exe with a fixed read-only script (Windows Update Agent history through COM, Win32_QuickFixEngineering through CIM; no update search, download or install); the tools report update titles, dates, outcomes, failure codes and support links, and hotfix ids, descriptions, install dates and the account that installed them, to the model; treat the output like the Settings app's own update history page.
entries.capability_summary: hermes-windows-updates (community, maintained by Yicheng-Mark) Answer "what did Windows install lately, and did it work" on Windows: the update history the Settings app shows - Windows updates, Defender signature and platform updates, driver updates - newest first, with each entry's outcome in words (in progress, succeeded, succeeded with errors, failed, aborted) and, when an entry did not end clean, the failure's error code in 0x form (the agent hands codes over signed; -2145124300 is shown as its unsigned spelling). Filter to the ones that did not end clean, or search titles. The hotfix list (KB numbers, security updates, install dates, newest first) answers "when was this machine last patched" at a glance; it carries OS-level updates only, which the notes say. Use it for "why does it say pending forever", for "did the update that broke something actually install", and for a patch report before assuming a machine is current. Read-only: the history is queried through the Windows Update Agent's session interface and CIM, and nothing else - no update search is run, nothing is downloaded, installed or uninstalled, no elevation. On the writing machine a 723-entry history returns the newest 500 in about a tenth of a second; the first call also starts the COM session, about a quarter of a second. The plugin declares no Python dependencies; there is no network call of its own and no file write. Windows only. Disclosure — each tool call runs one hidden powershell.exe with a fixed read-only script (Windows Update Agent history through COM, Win32_QuickFixEngineering through CIM; no update search, download or install); the tools report update titles, dates, outcomes, failure codes and support links, and hotfix ids, descriptions, install dates and the account that installed them, to the model; treat the output like the Settings app's own update history page. This plugin registers tool(s): win_update_history, win_hotfix_table. Platforms: windows. Requires Hermes >=0.21.4.

entries.name: hermes-witness
entries.description: Evidence-gated learning for Hermes Agent. Grades each agent-written skill against the session's real tool results, tracks outcomes in later use, and quarantines grade-D skills. Deterministic and local, no LLM calls. Disclosure — reads MEMORY.md, USER.md and skills under your Hermes home and grades every skill the agent creates or edits (including ones you wrote); in the default `gate` mode it moves grade-D skills to `~/.hermes/witness/quarantine` (reversible with `hermes witness release`); writes a local hash-chained ledger and a trace of tool names and argument keys only; no network calls, credentials, shell commands, background processes or telemetry. No dependencies, no self-updating code, no core overrides, no binaries. Release and trust are CLI-only.

entries.name: hermes-workbench
entries.description: The Hermes desktop app in your browser. `hermes workbench` serves the desktop interface through the Hermes dashboard, for headless servers, VPSes and tablets. Disclosure — community plugin, not a Nous product. On the first `hermes workbench` run and again after each Hermes update it runs `npm install --ignore-scripts` (guided by Hermes's lockfile) and Vite against your Hermes checkout's desktop sources, writing only under ~/.hermes/hermes-workbench and its own plugin dir (the checkout is only read), and starts `hermes dashboard` on loopback when none is running.

entries.name: hermes-workflows
entries.description: Agent-owned workflow graphs for Hermes — a background runner executes a JSON DAG of agent nodes, fan-outs (quorum) and human/machine gates with fingerprint replay-skip resume, cooperative steer, typed failure events and compact status payloads; ships a desktop DAG view, an inline transcript card and the authoring skill with measured budget recipes. Stock Hermes; no patched core required. Disclosure — every workflow run spawns a detached background runner (wf.py run <id>) that survives session end, gateway restart and plugin disable until the graph reaches a boundary or workflow stop; each agent node is a child hermes chat --query-file … --oneshot -Q … inheriting the runner's environment, and a node with profile set runs as that named profile (with its own credentials) only if the target's workflow_team.json lists the launcher; a gate's wait.until_argv and a fan-out's precheck_argv (run once per item before its child spawns) run agent-authored argv directly from the runner, outside Hermes' tool-approval gate (the engine uses no shell, but the shipped machine-watch and incident-response templates use until_argv to run a shell line read from a fixed-name handoff file under $HERMES_HOME, and release-lifecycle one read from a per-run handoff file in the run dir); the runner makes itself the subreaper of its children and SIGTERM/SIGKILLs any process a node leaves running (its own descendants plus pids registered in the run's .proctree_sidecar.jsonl) when the node finishes, retries or the run stops; run and amend send a one-token ping through Hermes' configured providers to check pinned model routes; at gate.held/run.done/run.failed/run.partial and fan-out straggler events the runner reads the API server key from config.yaml (or API_SERVER_KEY) and POSTs a wake turn to the configured Hermes API server — every wake states that it grants no new scope and revokes no existing authority; the run.failed and run.partial wakes ask the woken session to assess the run and, under its existing mandate, repair, amend or relaunch it when the task still needs it (those actions go through the session's normal tools and approvals), while the straggler wake asks the woken session to take one action (steer the open items, accept the partial, or stop the run); a transform_llm_output hook appends a ::workflow{id} card line to replies for runs the session launched in the last 30 minutes; the runner reads WORKFLOW_MAX_SEATS (that key only) from $HERMES_HOME/.env and the active profile's .env; state.db is read read-only, including every profile's session ids and profile names, and status/wait can read runs in sibling profiles' workflows dirs; opt-in settings (all default off) mirror run lifecycle events to an operator-configured https webhook with an optional bearer (outbound_bridge), present held gates into the run owner's own gateway session via plugin message injection (hooks_bridge_allow: approval_bridge, which also needs allow_gateway_injection), and append delegate_task child records to a spool under $HERMES_HOME/plugin-state (hooks_allow: subagent_accounting); every accepted launch also writes an executable shim at $HERMES_HOME/scripts/hermes-workflows-tick.sh and arms a single hermes-workflows-tick Hermes cron job (no_agent, so it wakes no agent; every 2m by default, tunable via WF_TICK_SCHEDULE or workflows.tick_schedule) that revives dead runners and deletes itself once no run is active — disabling or uninstalling the plugin mid-run does not remove the job or shim; state lives under $HERMES_HOME/workflows/ (or a configured runs_root). No other network of its own.

entries.name: hermes-wsl-terminal
entries.description: Run Hermes' terminal tools inside an existing WSL distro on Windows: one bash -c per command as the distro's default user, over the same files Windows sees at /mnt/<drive>, with no Docker Desktop, no image and no container to start or tear down. A host cwd is translated (C:\Users\me\proj becomes /mnt/c/Users/me/proj, \\wsl.localhost paths become the distro's own paths) and the mount root is asked once with wslpath, so a distro that moved its automount point still gets correct paths. cwd persists across commands, stdin and exit codes ride through wsl.exe, and hermes doctor / setup and the dashboard picker get real rows (wsl.exe path, WSL version, distros present, selected distro). HERMES_WSL_DISTRO and HERMES_WSL_USER select the distro and the user. Disclosure — this is a full-access backend, not a sandbox: when it is the selected backend, everything the terminal tool runs executes as your user inside your distro, with that distro's files, permissions and network access, so dangerous-command approval stays on and Hermes never stops the distro. The plugin itself reads no credentials, stores nothing and makes no network calls; it spawns wsl.exe per command and wslpath once per distro. It rewrites one core-produced string, the trailing cwd marker, because under WSL a command substitution is handed the directory wsl.exe started in rather than the shell's current one (measurements in the repo's VALIDATION.md); nothing in Hermes is patched or rebound at runtime.

entries.name: hermes-wslc-sandbox
entries.description: Run Hermes' terminal, file and execute_code tools in a Linux container on Microsoft's WSL Containers (wslc) runtime, so Windows users who run WSL Containers get a sandbox without Docker Desktop. Disclosure — the plugin spawns the wslc CLI (one short-lived process per command, plus one long-lived container per environment) and every call runs inside that container; containers have outbound network access unless docker_network is false; persistent sandboxes are left stopped on disk until removed; host environment variables enter the container only when named in docker_forward_env, and only paths listed in docker_volumes are bind-mounted. wslc rejects --cap-drop, --security-opt, --pids-limit, --init and --storage-opt, so this sandbox is not capability-dropped the way the Docker backend's is, container_disk is reported but not enforced, and dangerous-command approval deliberately stays enabled for this backend. The plugin reads no credentials, stores none, and makes no network calls of its own.
known_issues: container_disk is reported but not enforced: wslc has no --storage-opt.
No capability dropping: wslc rejects --cap-drop and --security-opt, so dangerous-command approval stays enabled.

entries.name: hermes-x-bookmarks
entries.description: Reads your own X bookmarks (long posts and X Articles in full) through the official X API with your own X app, sorts them with your Hermes model (category, tags, kind, priority, summary) and exports them to a board on your Desktop, Obsidian notes, a Notion database or a Google Doc. A weekly digest (best bookmarks numbered, 3 post ideas) arrives in your chat; reply "task 3" or "skill 2" to turn an item into a task or a Hermes skill. Disclosure — calls api.x.com (read-only, keys of your own X app from the Hermes .env via secret scope, or Hermes' X OAuth 2.0 sign-in, or `xurl token` when you pick the xurl sign-in, which runs that CLI); sends post text to your configured Hermes model; only when you export there: Notion through Hermes' Notion connector (ctx.call_mcp to the notion MCP server, only if you add it to this plugin's mcp_allowlist; creates the database, two boards and pages, updates those pages) or api.notion.com with an optional XBM_NOTION_TOKEN, and docs.googleapis.com through Hermes' Google sign-in (your own Desktop client, scope drive.file only); writes an 'X Bookmarks' folder on your Desktop (or export_dir) and notes into your Obsidian vault's 'X Bookmarks' folder, and reads Obsidian's obsidian.json to find the open vault; bookmarks, labels, export ids, digests, tasks and skill drafts are stored in plugin data; only on your command it creates one Hermes cron job (/xbm schedule, through cronjob_manage; it stays until /xbm unschedule) and Hermes skills (/xbm skill N save, through skill_manage, subject to Hermes' approval); a pre_llm_call hook adds a one-line note only to a message that is just "task N", "skill N" or "done N" after a recent digest; no credentials stored, no telemetry, no background process of its own.
entries.title: X Bookmarks
known_issues: You need your own X developer app on the pay-per-use plan; X bills your app for reads (about $0.001 per bookmark for owned reads; a first sync of ~1,900 bookmarks was about $1.89, and from 2026-11-22 X also bills expanded objects).
Notion export needs `hermes mcp install notion` and mcp_allowlist: ["notion"] for this plugin (or an XBM_NOTION_TOKEN); one chat export writes all pages and shows progress.

entries.name: hermes-xai
entries.description: The xAI API surfaces core does not cover, nothing it already ships (provider, x_search, web search, TTS, STT and Imagine stay in core). Voice module: full-duplex Grok Voice (grok-voice-latest) in the Desktop composer, built like core's GPT-Live mode; the voice model hands real work to Hermes as a normal turn on the open chat (surface voice-live) and reads the result aloud; the backend mints a 300 s xAI client secret so XAI_API_KEY never reaches the renderer. Collections module: one read-only tool, xai_collections_search, over documents the user already indexed in xAI Collections (GET /v1/collections, POST /v1/documents/search). Disclosure — the voice button captures microphone audio and streams it to api.x.ai over a WebSocket; the backend calls api.x.ai once per call with XAI_API_KEY (read through agent.secret_scope) to mint the secret; delegated requests run as normal Hermes turns with the profile's full toolset and approvals, and their final text (up to 3000 characters) plus the last spoken turns are sent back to xAI. Each xai_collections_search call sends the query to api.x.ai with XAI_API_KEY and returns passages into the conversation. Nothing is uploaded, stored or deleted and no telemetry is emitted; xAI bills on the user's key.

entries.name: hermes-zotero
entries.description: Search and read the papers in your own Zotero library before going to the web: a local, read-only full-text index (SQLite FTS5, BM25) built from a copy of Zotero's database, so it works with Zotero open or closed. Four tools (zotero_search with a strong/thin/none coverage verdict, zotero_read for passages, your own highlights and notes and a citation line, zotero_status, zotero_sync), a bundled skill that sends literature questions to the library first, and a `hermes zotero` command (doctor, snapshot, sync). Since 0.2.0, for users who supply their own Markdown conversions: tables are searched and read as tables (in_tables, mode=tables) and papers carry the flags ocr and text_damaged; the plugin contains no converter. Disclosure — reads outside its own data folder: the Zotero data directory (copies zotero.sqlite and its write-ahead log, reads the .zotero-ft-cache text files in storage/), Zotero's prefs.js to find that directory, and a Markdown folder only if the user sets one; writes only to its plugin-data folder (snapshot, index, lock file) and never to Zotero; the index holds the full text of the user's papers and stays on the machine; its only network request goes to Zotero's local API on 127.0.0.1:23119 for formatted citations, bypassing any proxy, and succeeds only when the user has switched that API on (off by default); no credentials, no shell commands, no background processes, no telemetry. Independent community plugin, not affiliated with Zotero.
entries.title: Zotero Library
known_issues: The first `hermes zotero sync` builds the index before the tools return results: about 3 minutes and 3.5 GB for 19,000 papers with full text (roughly 180 KB per paper); later syncs take seconds

Updating from an earlier version rebuilds the index once (0.2.1 does so to re-check every paper for damaged text): run `hermes zotero sync` after `hermes plugins update hermes-zotero`; until then the tools answer with the error index_outdated

Citations come from Zotero itself only while Zotero is running with its local API switched on (Settings → Advanced, off by default); otherwise the citation line is an approximate author-year line marked approximate: true
Search is lexical (BM25 with stemming), not semantic: synonyms and brand names can miss, and PDFs without a text layer are found by title and abstract only
Tested on macOS with Zotero 11; the Windows and Linux data-directory paths are implemented but not yet tested

entries.name: hermes64
entries.description: Author and edit room-based N64-era-style 3D games with story checks, bot playtests and local exports. Disclosure — Builds and playtests run Godot, Blender, Python and ffmpeg as local child processes (macOS: sandboxed, no network, writes confined to the game project; Windows: only after the owner opts into the Job Object runner, which has no network or write confinement). `/hermes64 setup --fetch --yes`, typed by the user, downloads SHA-512-pinned official Godot 4.6.2 files from github.com/godotengine (export templates about 1.25 GB) and clears macOS quarantine on the verified app. Hub downloads stay off until the owner sets `hub_url`. A `pre_llm_call` hook adds a hint steering game requests to Hermes64 into the user's turn, and the Studio tab can start a local 127.0.0.1 server for a web export or launch exported macOS/Windows builds.
entries.title: Hermes64
known_issues: Native Linux authoring is unavailable; native Windows is not verified for this release.
Requires standard Godot 4.6.2 and matching hash-verified export templates for exports.
Windows authoring requires the Job Object runner opt-in; it has no OS network or write confinement.
Windows cannot export macOS apps.
No general jumping, vehicle dynamics, multiplayer or seamless open world.
Image audits can fail on some style packs even when bots complete; agent-designed games may need iteration.
Godot setup is a human-confirmed download from official hosts; the optional export templates are about 1.25 GB.
macOS apps are ad-hoc signed, not notarized; Gatekeeper acceptance on other Macs is not established.
Validation (hermes plugins validate --install-deps) passes with one warning, a guarded hermes_cli import used for older-version discovery, and an in-process isolation note for one proof tool.

entries.name: hermes_otel
entries.description: OpenTelemetry for Hermes Agent: sessions, LLM and API calls, tool calls, sub-agents and approvals as OTLP traces, metrics and logs to any OTLP backend. Disclosure — sends span data including prompts, tool arguments and tool output only to backends you configure (a backends: list or an OTEL_* variable); by default content_capture is full and unclipped (preview clips to 1200 chars, off sends none); vendor SDK keys already in the environment are used only after that opt-in; with nothing configured it keeps a local owner-only SQLite store under $HERMES_HOME and sends nothing; installs opentelemetry-api, -sdk, -exporter-otlp-proto-http and -exporter-otlp-proto-grpc (>=1.35,<2) and PyYAML.

entries.name: hermesford
entries.description: An HD-2D pixel-art village page for Hermes Desktop: every chat is a villager who walks to the forge, library, woods or town hall depending on the tool its agent is running, waits at the town hall when the chat needs you, and goes home to sleep when the chat is not active. Click a villager to open its chat. Built on the Luminati engine (MIT). Desktop-only (desktop/plugin.js inside the plugin SDK surface, read-only session.list / session.active_list polling every 3 s); no agent tools, hooks, middleware, env vars or network calls.

entries.name: hermesmade
entries.description: Community bot shelf for Hermes. Add bots from hermesmade.lol in one click (hermes://open/hermesmade?add=<id>), share your own with /sharebot, and move your Grok Bot bots into Hermes, one Hermes bot each. Added bots are treated as untrusted: a package holding anything a share never includes is refused, its config is rebuilt from an allowlist (no hooks, approvals, terminal, plugins or model settings), schedules arrive paused, MCP servers arrive off, and every skill is scanned first. Each becomes its own profile on your model and login. Sharing and adding from the agent tool go through Hermes' approval prompt. Shares never include .env, auth.json, keys, tokens, memories or chats, and a single secret hit aborts the upload. Disclosure — network calls only to https://hermesmade.lol, when you browse, add, share or unshare (no telemetry, no install counting). Creates profiles under ~/.hermes/profiles. Keeps listing manage tokens in ~/.hermes/hermesmade/shared.json (0600). Reads profile secret values through agent.secret_scope only to block a leaking share (compared in memory, never stored or sent). Grok Bot migration reads grok-bot-export*.json from Downloads, makes no network calls, uses the official agent-importers plugin, and installs it with `hermes plugins install agent-importers` only after the user confirms.

entries.name: hermesvault
entries.description: Keep secrets out of plaintext .env files: a local encrypted vault (FloorVault, AES-256-SIV) whose items Hermes loads as environment variables at startup (mapped source "hermesvault", hv: references), with a hermes hvault CLI to manage items. The vault key lives in your OS key store (Keychain, Secret Service, DPAPI), a key file, a systemd-creds credential, or HERMES_VAULT_KEY. Disclosure — reads an encrypted store under <HERMES_HOME>/agent-vault (or secrets.hermesvault.dir) at startup; hermes hvault commands write to it and hermes hvault setup (or the first hermes hvault bind) creates it; hermes hvault bind also writes the secrets.hermesvault env mapping (an hv: reference, never the value) and enabled: true into the profile's config.yaml through Hermes' own config writer (--print-only prints it instead); hermes hvault bind and allow also keep a sealed binding record of each item's bound command lines in the per-user state directory (FLOOR_VAULT_STATE_DIR, else the platform's non-roaming state directory), outside the store; reads its own master key only from the variable named by token_env (default HERMES_VAULT_KEY) in the environment Hermes scopes to the profile being fetched, else from the custody set in secrets.hermesvault.custody: os (default; macOS Keychain, Linux Secret Service or Windows DPAPI, service floor-vault, shared with other FloorVault apps on the same account), key_file (the file named by secrets.hermesvault.key_file, which must not be writable by group or others), or systemd-creds (master.key.sdcred beside the store) — never from FLOOR_VAULT_KEY, VAULT_MASTER_KEY or FLOOR_VAULT_KEY_FILE, which it also protects from being overwritten; a configured custody that fails is reported, never replaced by another; a passphrase-protected store (floorvault 0.4) is not supported, because startup never prompts and never creates a key, a credential or a store (a locked or missing key is reported and Hermes starts without those variables), and only hermes hvault setup may unlock the key store or create the key; reads Hermes' own command line (sys.argv and sys.orig_argv, no other process's) to compare with the command bindings stored on an item by floorvault secrets allow or hermes hvault allow, and resolves a bound item only when Hermes was started with one of them (hermes hvault bind binds a new item to the command line Hermes starts its local gateway with, built from this interpreter and the profile home; --no-bind skips it) (secrets.hermesvault.require_binding, default off, also skips items with no binding); resolved values become environment variables of the Hermes process and its children, like .env entries; installs floorvault>=0.2.8,<0.5 from PyPI (plus secretstorage on Linux, pyobjc-framework-Security on macOS); one subprocess, only with custody: systemd-creds: the system's own systemd-creds (decrypt --user at startup; encrypt and decrypt in hermes hvault setup), found only in system directories, run as an argument list with no shell and a minimal environment, the key passed through a pipe; otherwise no subprocesses; no network calls, no self-update; protection is at rest, not against code already running as the same user.

entries.name: hermetic
entries.description: Status-bar popover for Hermes Desktop with three views: Costs (spend, cache, pricing drift, OpenRouter provider routing), AAI (skill changes, ratings, tests and replays) and HDR (a guard for risky tool calls, hooks, destinations, sensitive paths, what runs on its own). Disclosure: reads this profile's sessions (and other profiles' when you pick them) to audit tool calls, paths and hosts; can edit and save config.yaml and rewrite skill files when you apply a fix or revert a version, and once you give background tasks your routing rules, rewrites those tasks' entries in config.yaml by itself (from a background thread, at most once a minute) when the main provider changes; adds your data_collection and zdr routing rules to requests sent to Nous Portal; AAI replays and judge runs resend conversation context and tool definitions to OpenRouter with your OpenRouter key and incur cost (Nous Portal profiles are refused); trying a skill fix, only when you press it, drafts a new version and rewordings of your tests on your main model through Hermes' plugin model access and replays the tests on both versions (36 to 54 replays, estimate shown first), and never changes the skill until you press Apply; only when you turn them on, a background thread (every 5 minutes, inside $0.50 a day by default) replays your tests after the background review changes a skill and reverts that change if you chose revert, and tries a fix for a skill with 3 new failing tests without applying it; HDR lists listening TCP ports via ps/lsof; HDR's guard (off by default) checks each tool call through a pre_tool_call hook and, when you turn it on, holds calls Hermes does not check itself (reading keys and logins, writing startup items or key places Hermes does not list) and asks you in its own card, blocking without an answer in time (6 seconds inside Hermes' plugin hook limit: 24 seconds by default, 120 seconds when that limit is off) or at once when hermetic is not open, or blocks them outright; the guard is a best-effort match on the paths a call names, not a sandbox; questions from every profile wait in the default profile's hermetic folder; HDR also lists shell and gateway hooks and flags hook scripts edited after approval, keeping a copy of each script to compare; Costs reads public model price lists (OpenRouter, and hopscotchlabs.ai model pages for models a profile is billed for through Hopscotch) and, at most once a minute, asks Hermes for the profile provider's account report (OpenRouter usage and limits, Anthropic and OpenAI Codex plan windows, Nous credits and spend cap), with Hermes looking up the credential, and reads OpenRouter workspace and guardrail budgets itself with the profile's OpenRouter key, sent only to OpenRouter; once a day Costs reads OpenRouter's public endpoint list for the models in use and, with the OpenRouter key, the generation record of one recent call per provider for its exact model version, and only when you turn on its daily check, sends one tiny fixed prompt a day to each provider that served your models that week, through OpenRouter with your key and privacy rules; for Costs, HDR and AAI it also reads a few columns of each message straight from Hermes' session database, read-only, so a big history loads without opening every message; twice a day it reads hermetic's own plugin.yaml on GitHub and its catalog entry (no key) to say when an install is behind and Hermes will not update it; for a chat on another of the window's connections it reads that machine's chat list and the chat's /usage report through the plugin SDK, and on a Hermes whose SDK has ctx.restProfile asks hermetic's own backend on that machine, answering its guard questions there.

entries.name: hermis
entries.description: Disclosure — Windows only, not crypto. Runs a background WebSocket server on 127.0.0.1 (ephemeral port + session token) in a daemon thread. On the first autopilot or surface draw it launches a bundled transparent always-on-top Electron overlay as a detached process via npm (first run executes `npm ci` from the committed lockfile, downloading pinned npm packages and the Electron binary; disable with HERMIS_OVERLAY_AUTOSTART=0). The overlay obtains a short-lived interactive session ticket from the local Hermes gateway control socket and listens only to voice.status and wake.detected. It renders HTML/SVG blocks from replies in a sandboxed iframe that may load scripts from cdnjs/jsdelivr/unpkg, and loads https images. While Autopilot is on, the titles of up to 15 open windows are sent to your model provider on every turn. launch_app opens desktop apps by name only (shells, interpreters and paths are refused); with arguments or outside a small allowlist Hermes asks you first, except an allowlisted browser opening exactly one http/https URL, which opens without asking. layout_windows moves, resizes and focuses real windows via Win32 (user32); Store apps are found with a read-only powershell Get-StartApps lookup. Every child process gets an allowlisted minimal environment without provider keys. Optional camera gestures (off by default, Autopilot only) process frames locally with MediaPipe, and the model is downloaded once from storage.googleapis.com (SHA-256 verified). Reads config.yaml read-only and writes state.json, overlay.json, overlay.log and the gesture model to the plugin data dir.
entries.title: H.E.R.M.I.S
entries.capability_summary: hermis (community, maintained by gabogabucho) Disclosure — Windows only, not crypto. Runs a background WebSocket server on 127.0.0.1 (ephemeral port + session token) in a daemon thread. On the first autopilot or surface draw it launches a bundled transparent always-on-top Electron overlay as a detached process via npm (first run executes `npm ci` from the committed lockfile, downloading pinned npm packages and the Electron binary; disable with HERMIS_OVERLAY_AUTOSTART=0). The overlay obtains a short-lived interactive session ticket from the local Hermes gateway control socket and listens only to voice.status and wake.detected. It renders HTML/SVG blocks from replies in a sandboxed iframe that may load scripts from cdnjs/jsdelivr/unpkg, and loads https images. While Autopilot is on, the titles of up to 15 open windows are sent to your model provider on every turn. launch_app opens desktop apps by name only (shells, interpreters and paths are refused); with arguments or outside a small allowlist Hermes asks you first, except an allowlisted browser opening exactly one http/https URL, which opens without asking. layout_windows moves, resizes and focuses real windows via Win32 (user32); Store apps are found with a read-only powershell Get-StartApps lookup. Every child process gets an allowlisted minimal environment without provider keys. Optional camera gestures (off by default, Autopilot only) process frames locally with MediaPipe, and the model is downloaded once from storage.googleapis.com (SHA-256 verified). Reads config.yaml read-only and writes state.json, overlay.json, overlay.log and the gesture model to the plugin data dir. This plugin registers tool(s): autopilot, render_surface, close_surface, list_surfaces, layout_windows, launch_app; hook(s): pre_llm_call, pre_tool_call, post_tool_call, post_llm_call. Platforms: windows. Requires Hermes >=0.22.3.

entries.name: hicortex
entries.description: Shared fleet memory for Hermes agents: every connected agent learns from all other agents connected to the memory, wherever they run. Sessions across machines and harnesses are distilled into one common brain overnight — what one learns, the whole fleet recalls. Pushes a compact per-turn recall index (entries lazy-load via hicortex_get), injects fresh lessons plus a per-agent standing context block at session start — lesson blocks are delimited and carry an explicit reference-data framing line and provenance header — and exposes the full 9-tool memory surface (search, get, recent, ingest, lessons, index, graph, update, delete) through the shared server. The same server also serves Claude Code, OpenClaw, Pi and opencode agents, so mixed-harness fleets share one brain. Stdlib-only, no pip dependencies. Requires a running Hicortex server (npx @gamaze/hicortex init on any machine); data flow: each user message is sent to your configured Hicortex server for recall (default http://localhost:8787); session distillation runs on the server. Disclosure — sends every user message (and profile name) to your configured Hicortex server each turn for recall, default http://localhost:8787, plain http with a bearer token is accepted for remote servers with a one-time log warning; the server's standing Identity text and lessons are injected into the system prompt; the model can permanently update or delete shared fleet memories via hicortex_update / hicortex_delete without confirmation.

entries.name: hive
entries.description: Hermes remembers how its errors were fixed, and Hermes installs can share those fixes: when a terminal command fails with an error that was fixed before, Hive adds the fix that worked (with how often it worked) under the output. Fixes are learned from exit codes, not guessed: a failed command, the steps after it, and the same command succeeding. Opt-in, Hive trades fixes with other installs over Nostr, signed by a random per-install key, with proof of work, cross-checks and a safety screen; it never runs anything. Disclosure — reads terminal command text, exit codes and output through the transform_terminal_output hook and (on `hermes hive learn`) state.db read-only; stores learned fixes under plugin-data/hive; with `hermes hive network read` it sends error fingerprints (hashes) to the configured Nostr relays (default nos.lol, relay.primal.net, relay.damus.io) to look up fixes; with `network share` it also publishes the normalized error line and the fix commands (home paths, private paths, hosts, IPs, e-mails and secret-looking text removed or withheld; preview with `hermes hive outbox`). Network is off by default.

entries.name: holdings
entries.description: Holdings is a Hermes Desktop plugin that shows your crypto wallet and exchange balances in one place. You can review activity against the original records and export records with a note on what each source covers. Ask Holdings answers questions with your Hermes model and checks every cited number against your records. It is read-only and never signs transactions or moves funds. The demo uses fictional records and needs no keys. Disclosure — crypto portfolio viewer, read-only (no signing, transfers or trades). Sends the wallet addresses you add and your read-only exchange API keys (stored through Hermes secrets) to their own vendors: Kraken, Binance, Bybit, Etherscan, Zerion, GoPlus, public RPCs (PublicNode, dRPC, MEV Blocker, Solana mainnet), DefiLlama and GeckoTerminal. Saved wallet and exchange records go to your active model only after you enable `share_private_chat_tools` (off by default). Weekly briefing and alert watch cron jobs are opt-in templates.
entries.title: Holdings
known_issues: Protected reviews and Alert watch need Holdings to load in the Hermes process, with plugins.isolation set to in_process. When plugins run in the separate plugin host (plugins.isolation set to host), Holdings shows that protected reviews are unavailable. Saved reviews also need an external vault key, and a value typed only in plugin Settings stays locked.
The weekly briefing and the alert watch Cron job are opt-in templates. They never schedule themselves, and the scheduled weekly text lists section names only.
Device notification delivery was tested with fixtures only. A live look-alike case and real-model Cron delivery were not verified, and Zerion Ethereum 1Y charts returned unavailable in native QA.

entries.name: holographic
entries.description: Local fact-store memory provider: SQLite with FTS5 keyword search (word forms in English, Russian, Spanish, French, Portuguese, Indonesian, German, Hindi, Arabic, Bengali, Italian, Turkish, Polish and Dutch; Russian and English words of the same root at a lower weight, from bundled DerivBase.Ru (Apache-2.0) and Open English Wordnet (CC BY 4.0) pairs; German compounds and German and Spanish irregular verb forms from bundled Wikidata Lexemes tables (CC0); Chinese, Japanese, Korean and Thai by character n-grams, Chinese also split into words with jieba's dictionary (MIT), Traditional and Simplified Chinese compared as one through a bundled OpenCC table (Apache-2.0), Japanese spelling variants through SudachiDict's (Apache-2.0); synonyms through keywords the agent gives when it stores a fact), trust scores, entities with aliases and HRR (holographic reduced representation) recall, with no API key, network or model calls unless an optional online feature is switched on: search by meaning (embeddings: on) or rescoring by a cross-encoder (rerank: on), both off by default. The provider that shipped in-tree as plugins/memory/holographic, with the same provider name, config (plugins.hermes-memory-store) and memory_store.db, so `hermes update` moves existing users onto it; a file without merges keeps history schema 1; the first merge raises it to schema 2, after which writers of 0.15-0.18 refuse it until 0.19.0 or a pre-merge backup is restored. Taken over from Nous Research's handoff copy (NousResearch/hermes-plugin-holographic) and maintained by itpartypattaya; since 0.1.1 it fixes probe/reason/related/contradict, non-atomic writes and the never-written retrieval_count, gates recall by relevance without repeats, flags duplicates and conflicts when a fact is added, and honours the provider contract (read-only subagent contexts, hermes_home, mirror metadata, backup_paths); since 0.8.0 it keeps the history of every fact (change / end / correct / revert, search and list as_of a date) and `forget` erases a fact with all its versions from the file; since 0.16.0 a name guessed from a fact's text must be shaped like one and stays provisional until a second fact or a person confirms it, and entities can be renamed or deleted (the facts stay). Since 0.18.0 an optional, experimental second stage reorders the recall candidates with a cross-encoder at a /v1/rerank endpoint that answers in Cohere's shape without a key, such as llama-server (rerank: on, off by default). It does not raise hits: on the maintainer's held-out set (126 questions) it cut non-target facts in the top five by about 40 % and lines per turn by about a third, and lost about one target per hundred questions. Disclosure — local only unless an optional online feature (search by meaning or rescoring) is switched on: reads and writes one SQLite file per profile ($HERMES_HOME/memory_store.db unless db_path says otherwise), or with scope: user / chat / thread one file per user or chat in holographic-users/ or holographic-chats/ next to it; each fact version records where it was written (platform, chat type, chat and thread id, session id, the turn author's id and display name, and whether the person said it or the agent inferred it; never chat titles), shown in full by list, history and export and not in recall unless recall_source: short (date, display name, this or another chat); each confirmation of a fact by a person keeps its time, session id and that person's id (no text); forget deletes that and the confirmations with the fact and keeps only an HMAC of the text, keyed by a random key stored in the same file, as a tombstone; delete_entity removes a name, its aliases and links from the entity index (never a fact) and keeps an HMAC of each name the same way (not of an alias only a fact's text gave, which goes without one), and both rewrite the file so freed pages keep no copy; the first writable open after an upgrade that changes the extraction rules relinks the facts to their entities under the new rules (stores up to 2,000 facts and 500,000 characters; larger ones on fact_store rebuild_entities), changing only the names it guessed and their links, never a fact, a declared name or an alias someone gave; subagents never write, but a cron job's explicit fact_store / fact_feedback calls do unless cron_writes: false (on by default); no subprocesses or telemetry (at the debug log level the recall stages log fact ids and scores, never text), and no network calls or credentials unless embeddings: on or rerank: on (both off by default). entries.title: Holographic
known_issues: Word forms are matched by stems, not a dictionary: an irregular form can miss (ponies / pony). A synonym is found only if the fact's keywords name it, unless the optional online search by meaning is on; facts stored without keywords (older ones, auto_extract) need `enrich`.

Arabic, Indic scripts, Indonesian, German, Turkish, Polish and Dutch are matched by scanning the facts' text: the first such search after start analyses every fact (about 1-1.5 s at 5,000 facts, 4-6 s at 20,000); stores without such facts never scan. The bundled dictionaries load on the first word of their language (Chinese about 0.2 s and 30 MB).

forget cleans the database file only: Hermes session history, `hermes backup` archives and copies other tools made are not rewritten (tools can read the `forgotten` table and clean their own copies by fact id).

rerank: on is experimental and does not raise hits. On the maintainer's held-out set it lost one target in 126 questions with embeddings off and two with them on, on questions where several facts of one kind compete, against about 40 % fewer non-target facts. Each turn waits for one rerank call: on 4 CPU threads about 120 ms median with jina-reranker-v2-base-multilingual and 340 ms with bge-reranker-v2-m3, capped by rerank_timeout (3 s, lower with embeddings on so that both fit the core's 8 s prefetch budget). The suggested CPU model, jina-reranker-v2-base-multilingual, is CC-BY-NC-4.0 (non-commercial use only); bge-reranker-v2-m3 is Apache-2.0. The plugin ships no model. It sends no key, so a cloud rerank API that requires one (Cohere, Jina) refuses every call; it is tested with llama-server.

After the first merge the file uses history schema 2. Downgrading to a writer below 0.19.0 disables memory for that file until 0.19.0+ is restored or a pre-merge backup is used; manually lowering the schema mark is unsafe. There is no automatic unmerge. In this first release merged copies keep separate historical ids and confirmations are not pooled into the retained fact's origin counts.

memory_map.py (experimental, off unless run) writes the stored facts' texts to its output: a page or file made from it must stay behind a password and is not reached by a later forget. Its JSON format may change without a deprecation period. prefetch_clause_coverage (experimental, off) rescued no facts on one live install's history (5,081 messages) and is kept off there.
